Introduction to tidyEmoji

Youzhi Yu
University of Chicago

Source: vignettes/introduction.Rmd
introduction.Rmd

Overview

Emoji are everywhere in modern text (social-media posts, product reviews, chat and support logs, survey free-text), and they carry information that plain words do not. Yet summarising emoji from a corpus is surprisingly awkward. Unicode does not interact cleanly with regular expressions, not every code point is an emoji, and a single visible emoji is often built from several code points joined together. Counting “how many posts contain an emoji” or “which emoji are most common” by hand quickly becomes painful.

tidyEmoji removes that friction. It provides a small family of verbs that take a data frame and the name of a text column, and return tidy data frames that drop straight into a dplyr/ggplot2 workflow:

Task Function(s)
Summarise / filter emoji_summary(), emoji_filter()
Extract emoji_extract_nest(), emoji_extract_unnest(), emoji_tokens()
Count emoji_frequency(), top_n_emojis()
Categorise emoji_categorize()
Score sentiment emoji_sentiment()
Score emotions emoji_emotion(), emoji_emotion_label()
Custom lexicons emoji_lexicons(), register_emoji_lexicon(), emoji_score()
Translate emoji_to_text(), text_to_emoji(), as_emoji*()
Search the vocabulary emoji_search(), emoji_find(), emoji_keywords()
Describe a glyph emoji_properties(), as_emoji_canonical(), emoji_identical()
Coverage emoji_coverage()
Flags and places emoji_country(), emoji_subdivision(), emoji_flag()
Tallies emoji_from_counts()
Relate emoji_pairs(), emoji_cooccurrence(), emoji_ngrams()
Measure emoji_position(), emoji_density(), emoji_ratio()
Interpretation risk emoji_ambiguity(), emoji_risk(), emoji_flag_ambiguous()
Context emoji_context(), emoji_collocations()
Functional type emoji_type(), emoji_faceness(), as_emoji_type()
Time emoji_trend(), emoji_turnover(), emoji_seasonality(), emoji_version_profile(), emoji_adoption_lag()
Text-emoji mismatch emoji_incongruity(), emoji_congruence(), emoji_incongruity_profile()
Model features emoji_dfm()
LLM pipelines emoji_sanitize(), emoji_token_cost(), emoji_hidden()
Provenance emoji_provenance(), emoji_unicode_version(), emoji_unicode_releases()

Find the verb for your question

The same capability serves many research communities, and the table above is organised by what the verbs do rather than by what people ask. This is the other index. Every help page also carries the matching keyword, so help.search("accessibility", package = "tidyEmoji") finds the verbs for it.

If you are asking… Start with
How much emoji is in this corpus, and which? emoji_summary(), emoji_frequency()
How much of my corpus can a lexicon score? emoji_coverage()
Is this emoji the same character as that one? (forensics, eDiscovery) emoji_identical(), emoji_properties()
What do readers disagree about? (content QA, miscommunication) emoji_ambiguity(), emoji_flag_ambiguous()
Does the emoji contradict the words? (sarcasm, review helpfulness) emoji_incongruity(), emoji_congruence()
Which countries do these flags name? emoji_country(), emoji_flag()
What do the reactions on these pull requests say? emoji_from_counts()
Which emoji belong to a semantic field? (stimulus sets, L2 studies) emoji_find(), emoji_keywords()
Which words keep company with an emoji? emoji_collocations()
Which emoji cluster together? (networks) emoji_pairs(), vignette("emoji-networks")
How did emoji use change over time, and how fast were new ones adopted? emoji_trend(), emoji_adoption_lag()
What will a screen reader announce? (accessibility) emoji_to_text(), as_emoji_name()
Faces or objects? (crisis communication, marketing) emoji_type(), emoji_faceness()
What should a language-model pipeline do with emoji? emoji_sanitize(), emoji_token_cost()
Is something hidden in this text? (prompt injection, phishing) emoji_hidden(), emoji_sanitize()
How does a model’s own output use emoji? (LLM output auditing) emoji_ratio(), emoji_position()
What features does a classifier need? (stylometry, ML) emoji_dfm()
Which catalogue and lexicons produced this result? emoji_provenance()

Two design choices are worth highlighting:

  • Grapheme-aware detection. Detection is performed on whole grapheme clusters, so skin-tone modifiers (👍🏽) and zero-width-joiner sequences such as the family emoji (👨‍👩‍👧‍👦) are treated as a single emoji rather than being split into their component parts. This is illustrated in the extraction section.
  • Tidy by default. Every verb returns a tibble, follows the verb(data, text_column) convention, and supports unquoted column names, so the functions compose naturally with the pipe. Grouping composes too: the verbs that work a row at a time carry a group_by() through to their result, as dplyr::mutate() and dplyr::filter() do, while the ones that pool across rows – the counts, the co-occurrence tables, the time series – warn that they ignore it and return one corpus-wide answer. See ?tidyEmoji for the full contract.
library(tidyEmoji)
library(dplyr)

# The charts below need three packages that tidyEmoji only Suggests. A vignette
# has to build without its optional dependencies, so the plotting chunks are
# gated on this flag rather than assuming the packages are there.
has_plot_pkgs <- all(vapply(
  c("ggplot2", "forcats", "stringr"),
  requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE
))
if (has_plot_pkgs) library(ggplot2)

That gate covers building this vignette. It does not carry over to the script knitr tangles out of it, the one edit(vignette("introduction", package = "tidyEmoji")) opens: a chunk’s eval option is a build-time instruction and is not part of the extracted code, so introduction.R calls ggplot() unconditionally. Everything in it that uses tidyEmoji alone runs against the package’s declared dependencies; install ggplot2, forcats and stringr if you want to run the whole file.

That describes the script you get from an installed package, because the tarball is built on a machine that has all three. The gate is evaluated when the vignette is built, so if you rebuild it yourself without them, knitr comments those chunks out of the tangled script rather than emitting them.

Example data

Throughout this vignette we use oasst_messages, a sample of 1,485 messages from OpenAssistant Conversations (OASST2, released under the Apache License 2.0), bundled with the package: people asking an assistant questions, and people writing the assistant’s replies, between January and October 2023 and in 17 languages. Emoji are rare in real text, so the sample is stratified on them: about half the messages carry one, where about 1% of OASST2 does. The figures below describe this sample, not chat in general. ?oasst_messages says how it was drawn and screened. Nothing below is specific to it: any data frame with a text column will do.

oasst_messages %>%
  select(created_at, role, lang)
#> # A tibble: 1,485 × 3
#>    created_at          role      lang 
#>    <dttm>              <chr>     <chr>
#>  1 2023-01-17 21:57:59 prompter  en   
#>  2 2023-01-18 02:53:56 assistant en   
#>  3 2023-01-18 16:46:42 prompter  en   
#>  4 2023-01-18 17:53:42 prompter  en   
#>  5 2023-01-18 18:55:26 assistant en   
#>  6 2023-01-18 20:34:44 assistant en   
#>  7 2023-01-19 09:04:12 prompter  en   
#>  8 2023-01-19 10:42:54 prompter  en   
#>  9 2023-01-20 06:19:07 prompter  en   
#> 10 2023-01-20 19:14:58 prompter  en   
#> # ℹ 1,475 more rows

emoji_summary(oasst_messages, text)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   n_with_emoji n_total n_orphan_components n_invalid_flags n_unlisted n_hidden
#>          <int>   <int>               <int>           <int>      <int>    <int>
#> 1          750    1485                   0               0          3        0

The messages themselves live in the text column, which is the column we pass to each tidyEmoji verb, beside a timestamp (created_at), the writer’s role and the language (lang). The outputs below report what tidyEmoji finds in that column rather than printing the messages.

Detecting and summarising emoji

emoji_summary()

emoji_summary() answers the first question one usually asks of a new corpus: how much emoji is in here? It returns a one-row tibble with the number of entries that contain at least one emoji and the total number of entries. An entry is counted once regardless of how many emoji it holds.

summary_tbl <- oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_summary(text)

summary_tbl
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   n_with_emoji n_total n_orphan_components n_invalid_flags n_unlisted n_hidden
#>          <int>   <int>               <int>           <int>      <int>    <int>
#> 1          750    1485                   0               0          3        0

Here, 750 of the 1,485 entries (50.5%) contain at least one emoji.

emoji_filter()

emoji_filter() keeps only the rows whose text contains at least one emoji, preserving every original column. This is useful when you want to compare emoji-bearing and emoji-free text, or restrict an analysis to the emoji subset. (emoji_tweets(), its old name, is defunct: since 0.7.0 it stops with an error naming emoji_filter().)

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_filter(text) %>%
  nrow()
#> [1] 750

Extracting emoji

tidyEmoji offers three complementary ways to pull the emoji out of text, depending on the shape of output you want.

emoji_extract_nest()

emoji_extract_nest() leaves the data unchanged except for an added list-column, .emoji_unicode, holding the emoji found in each row. The original data structure is preserved, which makes this convenient as an intermediate step.

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_extract_nest(text) %>%
  select(.emoji_unicode)
#> # A tibble: 1,485 × 1
#>    .emoji_unicode
#>    <list>        
#>  1 <chr [0]>     
#>  2 <chr [0]>     
#>  3 <chr [0]>     
#>  4 <chr [0]>     
#>  5 <chr [0]>     
#>  6 <chr [0]>     
#>  7 <chr [0]>     
#>  8 <chr [0]>     
#>  9 <chr [0]>     
#> 10 <chr [0]>     
#> # ℹ 1,475 more rows

emoji_extract_unnest()

emoji_extract_unnest() returns a long, tidy table with one row per (entry, emoji) pair: .row_number records the position of the entry in the data, .emoji_unicode is the emoji, and .emoji_count is how many times that emoji occurs in that entry. Entries without emoji are dropped.

emoji_per_message <- oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_extract_unnest(text)

emoji_per_message
#> # A tibble: 1,284 × 3
#>    .row_number .emoji_unicode .emoji_count
#>          <int> <chr>                 <int>
#>  1          15 👍                        1
#>  2          32 🤓                        1
#>  3          39 😉                        1
#>  4          41 😊                        1
#>  5          46 ⛔                        1
#>  6          46 ❌                        1
#>  7          46 🌲                        1
#>  8          46 🏡                        1
#>  9          46 🐺                        1
#> 10          46 👧🏻                        1
#> # ℹ 1,274 more rows

We can use this to plot how many emoji each emoji-bearing entry contains:

emoji_per_message %>%
  group_by(.row_number) %>%
  summarise(n_emoji = sum(.emoji_count)) %>%
  filter(n_emoji <= 10) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n_emoji)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 10)) +
  labs(x = "Number of emoji in the message",
       y = "Number of messages",
       title = "Most emoji-bearing messages contain a single emoji")

About three emoji-bearing messages in four carry just one emoji, with a long, thin tail of more emoji-heavy ones: a handful of replies tabulate dozens, which is why the chart stops at ten.

emoji_tokens()

emoji_tokens() produces a “one row per emoji occurrence” table, the emoji analogue of a tidy-text token table. It keeps the original columns and adds the glyph (.emoji) together with its name (.emoji_name), category (.emoji_category) and sentiment score (.emoji_sentiment). This single call gives you everything needed for counting, joining and plotting.

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_tokens(text) %>%
  select(role, lang, starts_with(".emoji"))
#> # A tibble: 1,454 × 6
#>    role      lang  .emoji .emoji_name           .emoji_category .emoji_sentiment
#>    <chr>     <chr> <chr>  <chr>                 <chr>                      <dbl>
#>  1 assistant en    👍     thumbs up             People & Body              0.522
#>  2 prompter  en    🤓     nerd face             Smileys & Emot…           NA    
#>  3 assistant fr    😉     winking face          Smileys & Emot…            0.464
#>  4 assistant en    😊     smiling face with sm… Smileys & Emot…            0.645
#>  5 assistant ru    👧🏻     girl: light skin tone People & Body             NA    
#>  6 assistant ru    🔴     red circle            Symbols                    0.422
#>  7 assistant ru    🧒🏻     child: light skin to… People & Body             NA    
#>  8 assistant ru    🧑🏼‍🍳     cook: medium-light s… People & Body             NA    
#>  9 assistant ru    🌲     evergreen tree        Animals & Natu…            0.435
#> 10 assistant ru    🐺     wolf                  Animals & Natu…            0.263
#> # ℹ 1,444 more rows

A note on grapheme-aware detection

Modern emoji are frequently composed of several code points: a base emoji plus a skin-tone modifier, or several emoji joined by zero-width joiners. tidyEmoji detects emoji at the level of grapheme clusters, so these stay intact. The example below contains exactly two emoji (one family and one thumbs-up), and tidyEmoji counts them as such rather than splitting the family into four people or separating the thumb from its skin tone:

demo <- data.frame(
  text = c("our family \U0001F468‍\U0001F469‍\U0001F467‍\U0001F466",
           "great work \U0001F44D\U0001F3FD")
)

demo %>%
  emoji_extract_unnest(text)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   .row_number .emoji_unicode .emoji_count
#>         <int> <chr>                 <int>
#> 1           1 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦                        1
#> 2           2 👍🏽                        1

What counts, and what does not

The catalogue tidyEmoji detects against is Unicode’s own list of emoji, for the version emoji_unicode_version() reports, bundled with the package. Two kinds of emoji material are not emoji in it, and no verb counts them: a skin-tone swatch with nothing to modify (the tone after a grinning face, which cannot take one) and regional indicators that spell no country. emoji_summary() counts both, so they are accounted for rather than silently lost:

odd <- data.frame(text = c("\U0001F600\U0001F3FB",        # face + stray tone
                           "\U0001F1FD\U0001F1FD",        # "XX", no country
                           "\U0001F1EF\U0001F1F5"))       # Japan
emoji_summary(odd, text)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   n_with_emoji n_total n_orphan_components n_invalid_flags n_unlisted n_hidden
#>          <int>   <int>               <int>           <int>      <int>    <int>
#> 1            2       3                   1               1          0        0

Some emoji are also emoji only when they carry the presentation selector U+FE0F: the bare heart U+2764 is text, U+2764 U+FE0F is an emoji. Every verb that counts, scores or rewrites emoji takes presentation = "any" to read the bare forms as well (all but the copyright, registered and trade-mark signs, which are typography far more often than emoji):

hearts <- data.frame(text = c("I \u2764 R", "I \u2764\ufe0f R"))
emoji_summary(hearts, text)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   n_with_emoji n_total n_orphan_components n_invalid_flags n_unlisted n_hidden
#>          <int>   <int>               <int>           <int>      <int>    <int>
#> 1            1       2                   0               0          0        0
emoji_summary(hearts, text, presentation = "any")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   n_with_emoji n_total n_orphan_components n_invalid_flags n_unlisted n_hidden
#>          <int>   <int>               <int>           <int>      <int>    <int>
#> 1            2       2                   0               0          0        0

Counting emoji across the corpus

emoji_frequency()

emoji_frequency() counts how often each emoji appears across the whole text column (an entry containing the same emoji twice contributes 2) and returns the result sorted by descending count, annotated with each emoji’s name, shortcode and category.

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_frequency(text)
#> # A tibble: 398 × 5
#>    emoji name                            shortcode             group           n
#>    <chr> <chr>                           <chr>                 <chr>       <int>
#>  1 😊    smiling face with smiling eyes  blush                 Smileys & …   230
#>  2 😉    winking face                    wink                  Smileys & …    49
#>  3 😁    beaming face with smiling eyes  grin                  Smileys & …    34
#>  4 😄    grinning face with smiling eyes smile                 Smileys & …    30
#>  5 💰    money bag                       moneybag              Objects        28
#>  6 🤗    smiling face with open hands    hugs                  Smileys & …    28
#>  7 👍    thumbs up                       +1                    People & B…    25
#>  8 🤔    thinking face                   thinking              Smileys & …    23
#>  9 🙂    slightly smiling face           slightly_smiling_face Smileys & …    22
#> 10 😂    face with tears of joy          joy                   Smileys & …    19
#> # ℹ 388 more rows

top_n_emojis()

When you only need the leaders, top_n_emojis() is a convenience wrapper around emoji_frequency() that returns the n most frequent emoji (default n = 20).

top_20_emojis <- oasst_messages %>%
  top_n_emojis(text)

top_20_emojis
#> # A tibble: 20 × 4
#>    emoji_name            unicode emoji_category        n
#>    <chr>                 <chr>   <chr>             <int>
#>  1 blush                 😊      Smileys & Emotion   230
#>  2 wink                  😉      Smileys & Emotion    49
#>  3 grin                  😁      Smileys & Emotion    34
#>  4 smile                 😄      Smileys & Emotion    30
#>  5 moneybag              💰      Objects              28
#>  6 hugs                  🤗      Smileys & Emotion    28
#>  7 +1                    👍      People & Body        25
#>  8 thinking              🤔      Smileys & Emotion    23
#>  9 slightly_smiling_face 🙂      Smileys & Emotion    22
#> 10 joy                   😂      Smileys & Emotion    19
#> 11 smiley                😃      Smileys & Emotion    18
#> 12 wave                  👋      People & Body        16
#> 13 black_square_button   🔲      Symbols              14
#> 14 white_square_button   🔳      Symbols              14
#> 15 grinning              😀      Smileys & Emotion    14
#> 16 sweat_smile           😅      Smileys & Emotion    13
#> 17 rocket                🚀      Travel & Places      13
#> 18 cat2                  🐈      Animals & Nature     12
#> 19 clap                  👏      People & Body        12
#> 20 rofl                  🤣      Smileys & Emotion    12

Plotting the top 20, coloured by category, gives an immediate sense of how the community expresses itself:

top_20_emojis %>%
  mutate(emoji_name = stringr::str_replace_all(emoji_name, "_", " "),
         emoji_name = forcats::fct_reorder(emoji_name, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, emoji_name, fill = emoji_category)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Count",
       y = NULL,
       fill = "Category",
       title = "The 20 most frequent emoji")

The unicode column holds the actual glyph, should you wish to render the emoji themselves on a plot (this requires a graphics device with an emoji-capable font). You can also request a different number of emoji:

oasst_messages %>%
  top_n_emojis(text, n = 10) %>%
  mutate(emoji_name = stringr::str_replace_all(emoji_name, "_", " "),
         emoji_name = forcats::fct_reorder(emoji_name, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, emoji_name, fill = emoji_category)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL, fill = "Category",
       title = "The 10 most frequent emoji")

Categorising emoji

The Unicode standard organises emoji into 10 categories (see ?category_unicode_crosswalk). emoji_categorize() keeps the emoji-bearing rows and adds a .emoji_category column listing the distinct categories present in each row, separated by | when a row spans more than one.

msg_emoji_category <- oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_categorize(text) %>%
  select(.emoji_category)

msg_emoji_category
#> # A tibble: 750 × 1
#>    .emoji_category                                                            
#>    <chr>                                                                      
#>  1 People & Body                                                              
#>  2 Smileys & Emotion                                                          
#>  3 Smileys & Emotion                                                          
#>  4 Smileys & Emotion                                                          
#>  5 Animals & Nature|People & Body|Smileys & Emotion|Symbols|Travel & Places   
#>  6 Activities|Animals & Nature|Objects|People & Body|Smileys & Emotion|Symbols
#>  7 Animals & Nature|Food & Drink|People & Body|Travel & Places                
#>  8 People & Body                                                              
#>  9 Smileys & Emotion                                                          
#> 10 Smileys & Emotion                                                          
#> # ℹ 740 more rows

We can tally the most common category combinations:

msg_emoji_category %>%
  count(.emoji_category, sort = TRUE) %>%
  filter(n > 20) %>%
  mutate(.emoji_category = forcats::fct_reorder(.emoji_category, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, .emoji_category)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Number of entries", y = NULL,
       title = "Most common emoji category combinations")

To count the 10 individual categories rather than their combinations, split the .emoji_category strings on | with tidyr::separate_longer_delim():

msg_emoji_category %>%
  tidyr::separate_longer_delim(.emoji_category, delim = "|") %>%
  count(.emoji_category, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(.emoji_category = forcats::fct_reorder(.emoji_category, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, .emoji_category)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Number of entries", y = NULL,
       title = "Emoji category usage")

“Smileys & Emotion” dominates, followed by “People & Body”. Note that an entry spanning several categories is counted once in each, so these counts can exceed the number of emoji-bearing entries.

emoji_type(): faces versus everything else

The consumer-behaviour literature repeatedly contrasts emotional (face) emoji with semantic (object) emoji and finds that the two have different effects on engagement. emoji_type() recodes the Unicode group and subgroup into that smaller functional vocabulary, and emoji_faceness() reduces it to a single per-entry share:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_type(text) %>%
  count(.emoji_type, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   .emoji_type     n
#>   <chr>       <int>
#> 1 NA            735
#> 2 face          511
#> 3 gesture        50
#> 4 place          15
#> 5 nature         14

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_faceness(text) %>%
  summarise(mean_faceness = mean(.emoji_faceness, na.rm = TRUE),
            all_faces = sum(.emoji_faceness == 1, na.rm = TRUE))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   mean_faceness all_faces
#>           <dbl>     <int>
#> 1         0.719       511

as_emoji_type() is the vector-level version, for typing a glyph you already have in hand.

Scoring emoji sentiment

emoji_sentiment()

Emoji are a strong sentiment signal, and emoji_sentiment() surfaces it directly. It adds .emoji_n (the number of emoji in the entry), .emoji_n_scored (the number that appear in the lexicon), and .emoji_sentiment (the mean sentiment of the scored emoji, from -1 to +1). Scores come from the bundled emoji_sentiment_lexicon (described below); entries with no emoji, or whose emoji are not in the lexicon, receive NA.

msg_sentiment <- oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_sentiment(text)

msg_sentiment %>%
  select(.emoji_n, .emoji_sentiment)
#> # A tibble: 1,485 × 2
#>    .emoji_n .emoji_sentiment
#>       <int>            <dbl>
#>  1        0               NA
#>  2        0               NA
#>  3        0               NA
#>  4        0               NA
#>  5        0               NA
#>  6        0               NA
#>  7        0               NA
#>  8        0               NA
#>  9        0               NA
#> 10        0               NA
#> # ℹ 1,475 more rows

Sentiment distribution

Looking across the entries that contain at least one scored emoji:

msg_sentiment %>%
  filter(!is.na(.emoji_sentiment)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(.emoji_sentiment)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1) +
  labs(x = "Mean emoji sentiment",
       y = "Number of entries",
       title = "Emoji sentiment skews positive")

Emoji sentiment leans strongly positive, as it does in most text and more so here, where most emoji are an assistant being friendly.

Sentiment by category

Because emoji_tokens() attaches a sentiment score to every emoji occurrence, we can summarise average sentiment by category in a couple of lines:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_tokens(text) %>%
  group_by(.emoji_category) %>%
  summarise(mean_sentiment = mean(.emoji_sentiment, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_scored = sum(!is.na(.emoji_sentiment))) %>%
  filter(n_scored > 0) %>%
  mutate(.emoji_category = forcats::fct_reorder(.emoji_category, mean_sentiment)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(mean_sentiment, .emoji_category)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Mean sentiment", y = NULL,
       title = "Average emoji sentiment by category")

The sentiment lexicon

The scores come from emoji_sentiment_lexicon, the Emoji Sentiment Ranking of Kralj Novak et al. (2015), computed from around 70,000 tweets annotated in 13 European languages. You can work with it directly, for instance to find the most positive and most negative reasonably common emoji:

emoji_sentiment_lexicon %>%
  filter(occurrences >= 500) %>%
  slice_max(sentiment_score, n = 8) %>%
  select(emoji, unicode_name, occurrences, sentiment_score)
#>   emoji         unicode_name occurrences sentiment_score
#> 1     ❤    HEAVY BLACK HEART        8050       0.7460870
#> 2    💞     REVOLVING HEARTS         687       0.7423581
#> 3    🎉         PARTY POPPER        1125       0.7395556
#> 4    💃               DANCER        1344       0.7358631
#> 5    💙           BLUE HEART         912       0.7324561
#> 6    💖      SPARKLING HEART        1263       0.7133808
#> 7    💛         YELLOW HEART         602       0.7126246
#> 8    😘 FACE THROWING A KISS        3648       0.7017544

emoji_sentiment_lexicon %>%
  filter(occurrences >= 500) %>%
  slice_min(sentiment_score, n = 8) %>%
  select(emoji, unicode_name, occurrences, sentiment_score)
#>   emoji       unicode_name occurrences sentiment_score
#> 1    😒      UNAMUSED FACE        1385     -0.37472924
#> 2    😩         WEARY FACE        1808     -0.36836283
#> 3    🔫             PISTOL         604     -0.19536424
#> 4    😡       POUTING FACE         756     -0.17328042
#> 5    😔       PENSIVE FACE        1205     -0.14605809
#> 6    😞  DISAPPOINTED FACE         532     -0.11842105
#> 7    😭 LOUDLY CRYING FACE        5526     -0.09337676
#> 8    😴      SLEEPING FACE         718     -0.08077994

How much of the corpus can be scored?

A lexicon scores the emoji it was built from and nothing else, so before reading a sentiment result it is worth knowing how much of the corpus it covers. emoji_coverage() reports that for every lexicon at once, as a share of the emoji occurrences, as a share of the distinct emoji types, and as the number of emoji-bearing entries left with no score at all:

coverage <- oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_coverage(text)

coverage %>%
  select(lexicon, occurrence_coverage, type_coverage, n_rows_with_emoji,
         n_rows_unscored)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   lexicon    occurrence_coverage type_coverage n_rows_with_emoji n_rows_unscored
#>   <chr>                    <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>           <int>
#> 1 novak2015                0.750         0.613               750             135
#> 2 emotag1200               0.529         0.266               750             194

The sentiment lexicon scores 75% of the emoji occurrences here but only 61.3% of the distinct emoji, because a few common glyphs make up most of the occurrences. And 135 of the 750 entries holding an emoji have no .emoji_sentiment at all. Filtering those out before a comparison drops a sixth of the emoji-bearing data, and not at random: the unscored entries are the ones using the rarer glyphs. Report both coverage figures beside any lexicon-based result.

Interpretation risk: how much do readers disagree?

The most practically important fact about emoji is that people do not agree on what they mean. Miller et al. (2016) showed the same rendering to many readers and found they disagreed about whether it was positive, neutral or negative around a quarter of the time.

That disagreement was already inside the package. The Emoji Sentiment Ranking keeps the raw negative/neutral/positive annotation counts behind its collapsed score, which is an empirical interpretation distribution per glyph. emoji_ambiguity() reads it out:

emoji_ambiguity() %>%
  filter(n_annotations > 500) %>%
  head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   emoji key   n_annotations p_neg p_neu p_pos ambiguity  rank
#>   <chr> <chr>         <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl> <int>
#> 1 😳    1F633           846 0.327 0.327 0.345      1.10     6
#> 2 💯    1F4AF           637 0.281 0.317 0.402      1.09    16
#> 3 😴    1F634           718 0.422 0.237 0.341      1.07    43
#> 4 😢    1F622           749 0.385 0.224 0.391      1.07    47
#> 5 😱    1F631          1130 0.264 0.282 0.454      1.07    50

Because the measure is a property of the glyph, the corpus-level question – “which of my emoji are most likely to be misread?” – is one call:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_flag_ambiguous(text, top_n = 5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   emoji name                    n n_annotations ambiguity  rank
#>   <chr> <chr>               <int>         <int>     <dbl> <int>
#> 1 ❔    white question mark     1             9      1.10     1
#> 2 🎭    performing arts         1            15      1.10     1
#> 3 😳    flushed face            7           846      1.10     6
#> 4 💣    bomb                    1           131      1.09    10
#> 5 😲    astonished face         4           129      1.09    13

The default measure, entropy, treats the three annotation classes as unordered, so it scores an emoji whose readers split between negative and positive exactly as it scores one whose readers split between negative and neutral. The first is the one that causes real miscommunication. measure = "polarisation" respects the order: it is the expected distance between two readers’ judgements on a -1, 0, 1 scale, the statistic Miller et al. used, and it puts the face with open mouth and cold sweat at rank 6 of 969 where entropy puts it at rank 156.

emoji_ambiguity(measure = "polarisation") %>%
  filter(n_annotations > 100) %>%
  head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   emoji key   n_annotations p_neg p_neu p_pos ambiguity  rank
#>   <chr> <chr>         <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl> <int>
#> 1 😰    1F630           302 0.437 0.146 0.417     0.978     6
#> 2 😞    1F61E           532 0.479 0.160 0.361     0.960    12
#> 3 😡    1F621           756 0.533 0.107 0.360     0.958    16
#> 4 😢    1F622           749 0.385 0.224 0.391     0.950    18
#> 5 😫    1F62B           467 0.486 0.173 0.340     0.949    19

emoji_risk() is the per-entry version, and the pair .emoji_n / .emoji_n_scored keeps the coverage honest: an entry whose emoji are absent from the lexicon is not a low-risk entry, it is an unmeasured one.

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_risk(text) %>%
  filter(.emoji_n > 1) %>%
  select(.emoji_n, .emoji_n_scored, .emoji_ambiguity_mean,
         .emoji_n_ambiguous) %>%
  head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   .emoji_n .emoji_n_scored .emoji_ambiguity_mean .emoji_n_ambiguous
#>      <int>           <int>                 <dbl>              <int>
#> 1       10               7                 0.934                  2
#> 2        9               7                 0.811                  2
#> 3       14               4                 0.935                  1
#> 4        3               0                NA                      0
#> 5       11              10                 0.885                  5

The same counts also put an error bar on the sentiment score itself. A glyph annotated eight times should not carry the authority of one annotated eight thousand times, and emoji_sentiment(se = TRUE) says so:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_sentiment(text, se = TRUE) %>%
  filter(!is.na(.emoji_sentiment)) %>%
  select(.emoji_n_scored, .emoji_sentiment, .emoji_sentiment_se) %>%
  head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   .emoji_n_scored .emoji_sentiment .emoji_sentiment_se
#>             <int>            <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1               1            0.522              0.0161
#> 2               1            0.464              0.0171
#> 3               1            0.645              0.0104
#> 4               7            0.323              0.0408
#> 5               7            0.454              0.0601

Scoring emoji emotions

Valence (negative↔︎positive) is only one affective dimension. emoji_emotion() goes further, scoring each entry’s emoji across the eight Plutchik emotions (anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise, trust) using the bundled EmoTag1200 lexicon (Shoeb & de Melo, 2020). Scores are in [0, 1].

msg_emotion <- oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_emotion(text)

msg_emotion %>%
  select(.emoji_joy, .emoji_trust, .emoji_anger, .emoji_n)
#> # A tibble: 1,485 × 4
#>    .emoji_joy .emoji_trust .emoji_anger .emoji_n
#>         <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>    <int>
#>  1         NA           NA           NA        0
#>  2         NA           NA           NA        0
#>  3         NA           NA           NA        0
#>  4         NA           NA           NA        0
#>  5         NA           NA           NA        0
#>  6         NA           NA           NA        0
#>  7         NA           NA           NA        0
#>  8         NA           NA           NA        0
#>  9         NA           NA           NA        0
#> 10         NA           NA           NA        0
#> # ℹ 1,475 more rows

A quick way to read the result is the dominant emotion per entry:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_emotion_label(text) %>%
  count(.emoji_emotion, sort = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   .emoji_emotion     n
#>   <chr>          <int>
#> 1 NA               929
#> 2 joy              410
#> 3 trust             66
#> 4 anticipation      48
#> 5 fear              12
#> 6 sadness           11
#> 7 surprise           4
#> 8 disgust            3
#> 9 anger              2

The emotion scores join through the same codepoint-normalised key as sentiment, so emoji carrying the U+FE0F variation selector resolve correctly.

Bringing your own lexicon

Sentiment and emotion scoring share one pluggable engine. emoji_lexicons() lists the bundled lexicons (plus any you have registered):

emoji_lexicons()
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   name       type      dimensions     n source                           licence
#>   <chr>      <chr>     <I<list>>  <int> <chr>                            <chr>  
#> 1 novak2015  sentiment <chr [1]>    969 Kralj Novak et al. (2015), PLoS… CC BY-…
#> 2 emotag1200 emotion   <chr [8]>    150 Shoeb & de Melo (2020), EMNLP 2… MIT

emoji_score() is the generic scorer underneath emoji_sentiment(): give it any data frame with an emoji column and a score column (say, scores tailored to your own domain), and it returns the per-row mean, joined through the same codepoint-normalised key as everything else:

my_lexicon <- data.frame(
  emoji = c("\U0001f600", "\U0001f621", "\U0001f637"),
  score = c(1, -1, -0.5)
)

data.frame(text = c("great \U0001f600", "bad \U0001f621\U0001f637", "none")) %>%
  emoji_score(text, lexicon = my_lexicon)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   text     .emoji_n .emoji_n_scored .emoji_score
#>   <chr>       <int>           <int>        <dbl>
#> 1 great 😀        1               1         1   
#> 2 bad 😡😷        2               2        -0.75
#> 3 none            0              NA        NA

register_emoji_lexicon() stores a lexicon under a name for the session, so you can refer to it in emoji_score(), or in emoji_emotion() if it carries emotion columns:

register_emoji_lexicon("mine", my_lexicon)
emoji_lexicons() %>% filter(name == "mine")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   name  type   dimensions     n source          licence
#>   <chr> <chr>  <I<list>>  <int> <chr>           <chr>  
#> 1 mine  custom <chr [1]>      3 user-registered NA

Relating emoji: co-occurrence and sequences

Which emoji appear together? emoji_pairs() returns a tidy edge list: one row per pair of distinct emoji that co-occur in the same entry, with the number of entries in which they do. The item1/item2/n shape matches widyr::pairwise_count() and feeds directly into graph tools such as igraph, tidygraph and ggraph:

emoji_edges <- oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_pairs(text)

emoji_edges
#> # A tibble: 4,316 × 3
#>    item1 item2     n
#>    <chr> <chr> <int>
#>  1 🔬    🚀        4
#>  2 ☀️     ⛅        3
#>  3 ☀️     ⛈️         3
#>  4 ☀️     ❄️         3
#>  5 ☀️     🌊        3
#>  6 ☀️     🌤️         3
#>  7 ☀️     🌥️         3
#>  8 ☀️     🌦️         3
#>  9 ☀️     🌧️         3
#> 10 ☀️     🌨️         3
#> # ℹ 4,306 more rows

The strongest pairings make a readable chart on their own:

emoji_edges %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10) %>%
  mutate(pair = paste(item1, item2),
         pair = forcats::fct_reorder(pair, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, pair)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Number of entries containing both", y = NULL,
       title = "Emoji that appear together")

Set directed = TRUE to order each pair by first appearance, or supply doc_id to pool several rows (a conversation, a user, a day) into one document. emoji_cooccurrence(diagonal = TRUE) additionally returns each emoji’s document frequency on the diagonal.

Raw counts favour the common emoji, which pair with everything, and most pairs in a real corpus are seen exactly once. measure scores each pair against what its two emoji’s frequencies predict instead, and vignette("emoji-networks", package = "tidyEmoji") builds a network on it:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_pairs(text, measure = "dice") %>%
  filter(n >= 3) %>%
  head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   item1 item2     n  dice
#>   <chr> <chr> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 ⛅    ⛈️         3     1
#> 2 ⛅    ❄️         3     1
#> 3 ⛅    🌤️         3     1
#> 4 ⛅    🌥️         3     1
#> 5 ⛅    🌦️         3     1

Order also matters within an entry. emoji_ngrams() slides a window over each entry’s emoji in reading order (any text in between is ignored), which is the raw material for sequence and Markov-style analyses:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_ngrams(text) %>%
  count(.emoji_ngram, sort = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 579 × 2
#>    .emoji_ngram     n
#>    <chr>        <int>
#>  1 💰 💰           15
#>  2 🔲 🔲           10
#>  3 🔳 🔳           10
#>  4 🐑 🐑            8
#>  5 🍎 🍎            7
#>  6 🐈 🐈            7
#>  7 🔹 🔹            7
#>  8 👏 👏            5
#>  9 🐱 👢            4
#> 10 👢 💰            4
#> # ℹ 569 more rows

All the relational verbs canonicalise glyphs through the same codepoint-normalised key as the rest of the package, so qualified and unqualified forms of one emoji count as a single node.

The words around an emoji

Which emoji occurred is only half the story: emoji are polysemous, and their reading is decided by the co-text. emoji_context() returns one row per occurrence with a window of the surrounding text. Other emoji are blanked out of the window, so a neighbouring glyph never leaks into it:

notes <- data.frame(text = c(
  "so proud of the whole team \U0001F389 see you all on Friday",
  "missed the last train again \U0001F62D\U0001F62D walking home now"
))
notes %>%
  emoji_context(text, window = 4) %>%
  select(.row_number, .emoji, .emoji_context)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   .row_number .emoji .emoji_context                       
#>         <int> <chr>  <chr>                                
#> 1           1 🎉     of the whole team see you all on     
#> 2           2 😭     the last train again walking home now
#> 3           2 😭     the last train again walking home now

Aggregated over a corpus, those windows give the emoji-word associations that a sense inventory would otherwise have to supply – derived from your own data, so they are neither stale nor licence-encumbered:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_collocations(text, window = 4, min_n = 5) %>%
  head(10)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 4
#>    emoji word             n   pmi
#>    <chr> <chr>        <int> <dbl>
#>  1 🐈    котиках          8  5.55
#>  2 🐑    begin{matrix     9  4.90
#>  3 🐑    end{matrix       9  4.90
#>  4 🐑    left             9  4.90
#>  5 🔳    доски            7  4.71
#>  6 🐑    right            9  4.70
#>  7 🍎    manzanas         8  4.57
#>  8 🔹    замените         9  4.25
#>  9 🔲    больше          14  4.23
#> 10 🔹    игрового         8  4.23

Tokenisation stops at whitespace on purpose. If you need stemming or stopword removal, hand the result to tidytext rather than expecting this verb to grow a tokeniser.

Measuring how emoji are used

Where emoji sit and how much of the text they occupy are studied signals in their own right. emoji_position() reports each entry’s first and last emoji position and the mean relative position from 0 (start) to 1 (end):

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_position(text) %>%
  filter(!is.na(.emoji_rel_position)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(.emoji_rel_position)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05) +
  labs(x = "Mean relative position of the entry's emoji",
       y = "Number of entries",
       title = "Emoji cluster at the end of a message")

emoji_density() normalises the emoji count by text length (per character and per whitespace-delimited token), and emoji_ratio() reports what share of the text’s characters belong to emoji, including an .emoji_only flag for entries that are nothing but emoji (and whitespace):

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_ratio(text) %>%
  summarise(
    n_emoji_only = sum(.emoji_only, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_ratio   = mean(.emoji_ratio[.emoji_ratio > 0], na.rm = TRUE)
  )
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   n_emoji_only mean_ratio
#>          <int>      <dbl>
#> 1           19     0.0517

Emoji over time

Almost every substantive emoji study is longitudinal, and every message here carries the time it was written. emoji_trend() follows the most used emoji month by month, with the period’s total beside each count so the share can be recomputed for any grouping:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_trend(text, created_at, by = "month", top_n = 3) %>%
  filter(n_period > 50)
#> # A tibble: 12 × 6
#>    .period    emoji name                               n n_period  share
#>    <date>     <chr> <chr>                          <int>    <int>  <dbl>
#>  1 2023-02-01 😊    smiling face with smiling eyes    40      480 0.0833
#>  2 2023-02-01 😉    winking face                      15      480 0.0312
#>  3 2023-02-01 😁    beaming face with smiling eyes     9      480 0.0188
#>  4 2023-03-01 😊    smiling face with smiling eyes    51      262 0.195 
#>  5 2023-03-01 😉    winking face                      12      262 0.0458
#>  6 2023-03-01 😁    beaming face with smiling eyes     9      262 0.0344
#>  7 2023-04-01 😊    smiling face with smiling eyes    72      422 0.171 
#>  8 2023-04-01 😉    winking face                      17      422 0.0403
#>  9 2023-04-01 😁    beaming face with smiling eyes    10      422 0.0237
#> 10 2023-05-01 😊    smiling face with smiling eyes    25      158 0.158 
#> 11 2023-05-01 😁    beaming face with smiling eyes     2      158 0.0127
#> 12 2023-05-01 😉    winking face                       2      158 0.0127

emoji_turnover() asks a different question – not how often an emoji is used but how much of the repertoire changes from one period to the next:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_turnover(text, created_at, by = "month")
#> # A tibble: 9 × 8
#>   .period    .period_prev n_types_prev n_types jaccard n_new n_lost n_core
#>   <date>     <date>              <int>   <int>   <dbl> <int>  <int>  <int>
#> 1 2023-02-01 2023-01-01              1     204 0.00490   203      0      1
#> 2 2023-03-01 2023-02-01            204     111 0.230      52    145     59
#> 3 2023-04-01 2023-03-01            111     168 0.187     124     67     44
#> 4 2023-05-01 2023-04-01            168      82 0.208      39    125     43
#> 5 2023-06-01 2023-05-01             82      11 0.0333      8     79      3
#> 6 2023-07-01 2023-06-01             11      14 0.0417     13     10      1
#> 7 2023-08-01 2023-07-01             14       7 0.05        6     13      1
#> 8 2023-09-01 2023-08-01              7      16 0          16      7      0
#> 9 2023-10-01 2023-09-01             16      16 0.0323     15     15      1

The sample is stratified on emoji presence, so its monthly totals follow how many messages OASST2 collected each month, not how often people used emoji: use the counts to compare emoji with each other within a month, and read the totals as the sample’s, not the world’s.

Two of the time verbs read their time axis off the reference table, which already records the Unicode version that introduced each glyph. emoji_version_profile() needs no timestamp at all as a result, so “how new is this corpus’s emoji vocabulary?” is a single call:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_version_profile(text) %>%
  head(8)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 7
#>   version version_num release_date n_types n_tokens share_types share_tokens
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <date>         <int>    <int>       <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 0.6             0.6 2010-10-11       215      982      0.540       0.675  
#> 2 0.7             0.7 2014-06-16        24       64      0.0603      0.0440 
#> 3 1.0             1   2015-06-09        67      238      0.168       0.164  
#> 4 2.0             2   2015-11-12        12       14      0.0302      0.00963
#> 5 3.0             3   2016-06-21        20       41      0.0503      0.0282 
#> 6 4.0             4   2016-11-22        13       23      0.0327      0.0158 
#> 7 5.0             5   2017-06-20        22       53      0.0553      0.0365 
#> 8 11.0           11   2018-06-05         9       15      0.0226      0.0103

With real timestamps, emoji_adoption_lag() goes one step further and compares each glyph’s first appearance in the corpus with its Unicode release date – see emoji_unicode_releases() for that lookup, and emoji_seasonality() for month-of-year, day-of-week and hour-of-day cycles:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_adoption_lag(text, created_at) %>%
  arrange(lag_days) %>%
  head(5)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   emoji name                          n version release_date first_seen lag_days
#>   <chr> <chr>                     <int> <chr>   <date>       <date>        <int>
#> 1 🫥    dotted line face              4 14.0    2021-09-14   2023-02-08      512
#> 2 🫄🏾    pregnant person: medium-…     2 14.0    2021-09-14   2023-02-12      516
#> 3 🫣    face with peeking eye         1 14.0    2021-09-14   2023-04-16      579
#> 4 🫡    saluting face                 3 14.0    2021-09-14   2023-04-17      580
#> 5 🥷    ninja                         3 13.0    2020-03-10   2023-02-04     1061

Emoji as model features

For classification and regression work, emoji_dfm() turns the corpus into a document-by-emoji feature table: one row per entry (or per doc_id), one column per emoji, weighted by counts, binary presence or tf-idf. Every entry is kept (emoji-free rows are all zeros), so the table binds row-for-row to your outcome columns:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_dfm(text, weighting = "tfidf") %>%
  select(1:6)
#> # A tibble: 1,485 × 6
#>    .row_number  `😊`  `😉`  `😁`  `😄`  `💰`
#>          <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1           1     0     0     0     0     0
#>  2           2     0     0     0     0     0
#>  3           3     0     0     0     0     0
#>  4           4     0     0     0     0     0
#>  5           5     0     0     0     0     0
#>  6           6     0     0     0     0     0
#>  7           7     0     0     0     0     0
#>  8           8     0     0     0     0     0
#>  9           9     0     0     0     0     0
#> 10          10     0     0     0     0     0
#> # ℹ 1,475 more rows

Text-emoji mismatch

Two separate literatures converge on one statistic. NLP sarcasm detection uses emoji-text sentiment incongruity as a feature; marketing research finds that a mismatch between a review’s words and its emoji lowers perceived helpfulness and authenticity. Both want the same number.

tidyEmoji deliberately does not score text – that choice belongs in your script, where the method is visible. Here is a deliberately crude word-list scorer standing in for tidytext + AFINN, sentimentr or a transformer:

positive <- c("love", "great", "best", "happy", "good", "thanks", "beautiful")
negative <- c("hate", "worst", "bad", "sad", "awful", "sick", "tired")

scored <- oasst_messages %>%
  mutate(text_score = vapply(
    strsplit(tolower(text), "[^a-z]+"),
    function(w) as.numeric(sum(w %in% positive) - sum(w %in% negative)),
    numeric(1)
  ))

scale has no default: AFINN runs -5 to 5, VADER -1 to 1, and a model’s logits on nothing in particular, so you have to say how the two sides were made comparable. "rank" puts both on percentiles and is the safest choice.

The word list above keeps this vignette runnable on the package’s own dependencies, but it is not what you would use. Here is the same step with a real scorer, left unevaluated so that nothing here depends on it. Both produce a text_score column, and emoji_incongruity() does not care which:

# tidytext + AFINN: one score per matched word, summed per document
library(tidytext)
library(dplyr)

afinn <- tidytext::get_sentiments("afinn")     # prompts to download once

scored <- oasst_messages %>%
  mutate(.doc = row_number()) %>%
  tidytext::unnest_tokens(word, text, drop = FALSE) %>%
  inner_join(afinn, by = "word") %>%
  group_by(.doc) %>%
  summarise(text_score = sum(value), .groups = "drop") %>%
  right_join(mutate(oasst_messages, .doc = row_number()), by = ".doc") %>%
  mutate(text_score = tidyr::replace_na(text_score, 0))

# sentimentr, which scores sentences and handles negation and amplifiers
scored <- oasst_messages %>%
  mutate(text_score = sentimentr::sentiment_by(text)$ave_sentiment)

Two R packages take the opposite design, and both are complements rather than alternatives. EmojiSentR (Hanson, Lahrim and Tong, 2026) scores text and emoji together: it extracts the emoji, scores the words and the emoji separately, applies VADER’s negation rules and returns one weighted composite per document. That composite is a finished answer, where tidyEmoji keeps the two channels apart precisely so their disagreement can be measured: feed EmojiSentR’s word-channel score in as text_score and the two packages compose. text2emotion runs the other way round entirely: it classifies the emotion of the words with a trained model and maps the prediction onto an emoji for display, so it adds emoji to text rather than reading the emoji already there.

Either way, pass scale = "rank" unless you can say why the two scales are already comparable.

The percentiles are taken over the rows the comparison is defined on – those with both a scorable emoji and a text score – not over the whole corpus. Only 615 of these 1485 messages qualify, and ranking the text score against all 1485 would compare a percentile of one population with a percentile of another. One consequence is a useful sanity check: on the rank scale the mean gap over the scored rows is exactly zero, so a non-zero mean means your filtering, not your data.

incong <- scored %>%
  emoji_incongruity(text, text_score, scale = "rank")

incong %>%
  filter(!is.na(.emoji_incongruity)) %>%
  count(.emoji_polarity_flip)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   .emoji_polarity_flip     n
#>   <lgl>                <int>
#> 1 FALSE                  610
#> 2 TRUE                     5

incong %>%
  filter(.emoji_polarity_flip) %>%
  select(.emoji_sentiment, text_score) %>%
  head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   .emoji_sentiment text_score
#>              <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1           0.645          -1
#> 2           0.268          -1
#> 3          -0.0934          1

Note what happens to entries with no scorable emoji: they get NA, never 0. A neutral emoji and no emoji at all are different states, and collapsing them biases every model downstream. emoji_incongruity_profile() aggregates the same numbers by glyph, and emoji_congruence() is the identical engine under the marketing framing.

scored %>%
  emoji_incongruity_profile(text, text_score, scale = "rank", min_n = 10)
#> # A tibble: 18 × 7
#>    emoji name                n mean_incongruity sd_incongruity n_flips flip_rate
#>    <chr> <chr>           <int>            <dbl>          <dbl>   <int>     <dbl>
#>  1 😊    smiling face w…   230           0.521          0.343        2   0.00870
#>  2 😉    winking face       49          -0.278          0.304        0   0      
#>  3 😁    beaming face w…    34          -0.398          0.249        0   0      
#>  4 😄    grinning face …    30          -0.484          0.308        0   0      
#>  5 💰    money bag          28          -0.498          0.129        0   0      
#>  6 👍    thumbs up          25          -0.161          0.505        0   0      
#>  7 😂    face with tear…    19          -0.722          0.187        0   0      
#>  8 😃    grinning face …    18           0.0116         0.354        0   0      
#>  9 👋    waving hand        16          -0.451          0.271        0   0      
#> 10 🔲    black square b…    14          -0.205          0            0   0      
#> 11 🔳    white square b…    14          -0.205          0            0   0      
#> 12 😀    grinning face      14          -0.0355         0.440        0   0      
#> 13 😅    grinning face …    13          -0.840          0.280        0   0      
#> 14 🚀    rocket             13           0.156          0.658        0   0      
#> 15 🐈    cat                12          -0.510          0.212        0   0      
#> 16 👏    clapping hands     12          -0.0501         0.322        0   0      
#> 17 🔥    fire               11          -0.571          0.0878       0   0      
#> 18 🐑    ewe                10          -0.920          0            0   0

Translating emoji to and from text

Replacing emoji with words is useful for accessibility (screen readers) and as an NLP normalisation step before tokenising. emoji_to_text() does this for a whole column, in either Unicode-name or shortcode form; text_to_emoji() is the inverse.

demo <- data.frame(text = "great \U0001f600 love \u2764\ufe0f")
demo %>% emoji_to_text(text, format = "name")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   text                              
#>   <chr>                             
#> 1 great grinning face love red heart
demo %>% emoji_to_text(text, format = "shortcode")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   text                         
#>   <chr>                        
#> 1 great :grinning: love :heart:
demo %>%
  emoji_to_text(text, format = "shortcode") %>%
  text_to_emoji(text)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   text           
#>   <chr>          
#> 1 great 😀 love ❤️

Note that the qualified heart (which carries the U+FE0F variation selector) translates just as reliably as any other emoji, thanks to the normalised join key. For ad-hoc, vector-level use there are also as_emoji_name(), as_emoji_shortcode() and as_emoji():

as_emoji_name(c("\U0001f600", "\u2764\ufe0f"))
#> [1] "grinning face" "red heart"
as_emoji_shortcode(c("\U0001f600", "\u2764\ufe0f"))
#> [1] "grinning" "heart"
as_emoji(c("grinning", "heart"))
#> [1] "😀" "❤️"

Searching the emoji catalogue

emoji_search() looks emoji up by keyword, name or shortcode (case-insensitive, literal matching), returning a tidy tibble you can filter further or feed into the other verbs:

emoji_search("happy")
#> # A tibble: 27 × 5
#>    emoji name                            shortcode             group     keyword
#>    <chr> <chr>                           <chr>                 <chr>     <chr>  
#>  1 😀    grinning face                   grinning              Smileys … happy  
#>  2 😃    grinning face with big eyes     smiley                Smileys … happy  
#>  3 😄    grinning face with smiling eyes smile                 Smileys … happy  
#>  4 😁    beaming face with smiling eyes  grin                  Smileys … happy  
#>  5 😆    grinning squinting face         laughing              Smileys … happy  
#>  6 🤣    rolling on the floor laughing   rofl                  Smileys … happy  
#>  7 😂    face with tears of joy          joy                   Smileys … happy  
#>  8 🙂    slightly smiling face           slightly_smiling_face Smileys … happy  
#>  9 😇    smiling face with halo          innocent              Smileys … happy  
#> 10 ☺     smiling face                    smiling_face          Smileys … happy  
#> # ℹ 17 more rows
emoji_search("celebration")
#> # A tibble: 27 × 5
#>    emoji name                     shortcode      group             keyword    
#>    <chr> <chr>                    <chr>          <chr>             <chr>      
#>  1 🥳    partying face            partying_face  Smileys & Emotion celebration
#>  2 🙌    raising hands            raised_hands   People & Body     celebration
#>  3 🎅    Santa Claus              santa          People & Body     celebration
#>  4 🤶    Mrs. Claus               mrs_claus      People & Body     celebration
#>  5 🧑‍🎄    Mx Claus                 mx_claus       People & Body     celebration
#>  6 🎂    birthday cake            birthday       Food & Drink      celebration
#>  7 🍾    bottle with popping cork champagne      Food & Drink      celebration
#>  8 🎃    jack-o-lantern           jack_o_lantern Activities        celebration
#>  9 🎄    Christmas tree           christmas_tree Activities        celebration
#> 10 🎆    fireworks                fireworks      Activities        celebration
#> # ℹ 17 more rows

emoji_find() goes the other way, from a semantic field to its emoji, which is how a stimulus set is assembled; it matches whole CLDR keywords, and emoji_keywords() returns those keywords in long form:

emoji_find(c("party", "celebration"))
#> # A tibble: 36 × 5
#>    emoji name                     group             matched            n_matched
#>    <chr> <chr>                    <chr>             <chr>                  <int>
#>  1 🥳    partying face            Smileys & Emotion party, celebration         2
#>  2 🎂    birthday cake            Food & Drink      party, celebration         2
#>  3 🎈    balloon                  Activities        party, celebration         2
#>  4 🎉    party popper             Activities        party, celebration         2
#>  5 🎊    confetti ball            Activities        party, celebration         2
#>  6 🪅    piñata                   Activities        party, celebration         2
#>  7 😛    face with tongue         Smileys & Emotion party                      1
#>  8 😜    winking face with tongue Smileys & Emotion party                      1
#>  9 🙌    raising hands            People & Body     celebration                1
#> 10 🎅    Santa Claus              People & Body     celebration                1
#> # ℹ 26 more rows
emoji_keywords("\U0001F389")
#> # A tibble: 10 × 3
#>    emoji name         keyword    
#>    <chr> <chr>        <chr>      
#>  1 🎉    party popper awesome    
#>  2 🎉    party popper birthday   
#>  3 🎉    party popper celebrate  
#>  4 🎉    party popper celebration
#>  5 🎉    party popper excited    
#>  6 🎉    party popper hooray     
#>  7 🎉    party popper party      
#>  8 🎉    party popper popper     
#>  9 🎉    party popper tada       
#> 10 🎉    party popper woohoo

The keywords are the English CLDR sets, from the emoji package, so an emoji newer than that package has a name but no keywords.

What the catalogue knows about a glyph

emoji_properties() reports everything the catalogue records about a glyph: its code points, its qualification status, its name, group and subgroup, the Unicode version that introduced it, and whether it takes a skin tone. Called with no argument it returns the whole catalogue:

emoji_properties(c("\u2764", "\u2764\ufe0f", "\U0001F44D\U0001F3FD"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 11
#>   emoji codepoints      n_codepoints key     name  status group subgroup version
#>   <chr> <chr>                  <int> <chr>   <chr> <chr>  <chr> <chr>    <chr>  
#> 1 ❤     U+2764                     1 2764    red … unqua… Smil… heart    0.6    
#> 2 ❤️     U+2764 U+FE0F              2 2764    red … fully… Smil… heart    0.6    
#> 3 👍🏽    U+1F44D U+1F3FD            2 1F44D … thum… fully… Peop… hand-fi… 1.0    
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: modifiable <lgl>, has_fe0f <lgl>

Two spellings of one emoji differ only in U+FE0F, which makes a plain join on the glyph miss rows. as_emoji_canonical() maps every spelling to the one the catalogue marks fully qualified, and emoji_identical() says whether two glyphs are the same emoji, and how they differ when they are not:

as_emoji_canonical(c("\u2764", "\u2764\ufe0f"))
#> [1] "❤️" "❤️"
emoji_identical(c("\u2764", "\U0001F44D"),
                c("\u2764\ufe0f", "\U0001F44D\U0001F3FD"),
                details = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   x     y     identical exact difference         x_codepoints y_codepoints   
#>   <chr> <chr> <lgl>     <lgl> <chr>              <chr>        <chr>          
#> 1 ❤     ❤️     TRUE      FALSE variation selector U+2764       U+2764 U+FE0F  
#> 2 👍    👍🏽    FALSE     FALSE skin tone          U+1F44D      U+1F44D U+1F3FD

emoji_identical() compares code points. It cannot say what anyone saw, because rendering belongs to the font and the platform; its help page says so in full, and anyone using it as evidence should read it.

Flags and places

A flag emoji is two regional-indicator letters, so the country code is arithmetic, and the catalogue’s 259 country flags say which pairs are real. emoji_country() returns one row per flag with its ISO 3166-1 code, ready to join to a map or to countrycode::countrycode():

places <- data.frame(
  id = 1:2,
  text = c("Tokyo \U0001F1EF\U0001F1F5 then Paris \U0001F1EB\U0001F1F7",
           "stray \U0001F1FD\U0001F1FD letters"))
emoji_country(places, text)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>      id text               .emoji .emoji_iso2 .emoji_country_name .emoji_iso3166
#>   <int> <chr>              <chr>  <chr>       <chr>               <lgl>         
#> 1     1 Tokyo 🇯🇵 then Pari… 🇯🇵     JP          Japan               TRUE          
#> 2     1 Tokyo 🇯🇵 then Pari… 🇫🇷     FR          France              TRUE          
#> 3     2 stray 🇽🇽 letters   🇽🇽     NA          NA                  NA
emoji_flag(c("JP", "fr", "GB-SCT"))
#> [1] "🇯🇵" "🇫🇷" "🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿"

A pair that spells no country keeps its row and its glyph, with NA for the code. emoji_subdivision() does the same for the tag-sequence flags of England, Scotland and Wales.

Reaction data and other tallies

Reactions arrive as counts, not text: one row per item, emoji and number of presses. emoji_from_counts() writes each item’s tally out as text, so every verb above reads it. It understands GitHub’s reaction names as well as glyphs and shortcodes:

reactions <- data.frame(pr = c(101, 101, 102),
                        reaction = c("+1", "rocket", "-1"),
                        count = c(3, 1, 2))
reaction_text <- emoji_from_counts(reactions, reaction, count, id = pr)
reaction_text
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>      pr text       
#>   <dbl> <chr>      
#> 1   101 👍 👍 👍 🚀
#> 2   102 👎 👎
emoji_sentiment(reaction_text, text)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>      pr text        .emoji_n .emoji_n_scored .emoji_sentiment
#>   <dbl> <chr>          <int>           <int>            <dbl>
#> 1   101 👍 👍 👍 🚀        4               4            0.523
#> 2   102 👎 👎              2               2           -0.190

Real tally data is messier. OASST2 records reactions on its messages, and oasst_reactions holds them for the sample. Beside the two votes ("+1" and "-1") sit a report button ("red_flag") and the interface’s skip actions, none of which is an emoji. By default a value that resolves to no emoji is an error, because dropping it silently would change the answer; unknown = "drop" sets such rows aside and says which, with the counts they carried:

oasst_reactions %>%
  emoji_from_counts(reaction, n, id = message_id, unknown = "drop") %>%
  emoji_frequency(text)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   emoji name        shortcode group             n
#>   <chr> <chr>       <chr>     <chr>         <int>
#> 1 👍    thumbs up   +1        People & Body  2323
#> 2 👎    thumbs down -1        People & Body   802

The text is built so that every counting verb gives exactly the answer the tally implies. What it cannot do is say more than the tally does: a platform offering eight reactions records which of eight buttons was pressed, not what the reader felt.

Emoji in language-model pipelines

Emoji are now a preprocessing decision in every LLM pipeline, and the decision matters: they inflate token counts several-fold, and models disambiguate them poorly. emoji_token_cost() gives the exact sizes plus a clearly-labelled estimate – pass your real tokeniser through tokenizer when the number matters:

oasst_messages %>%
  emoji_token_cost(text) %>%
  filter(.emoji_n > 0) %>%
  summarise(emoji = sum(.emoji_n),
            bytes = sum(.emoji_bytes),
            codepoints = sum(.emoji_codepoints),
            est_tokens = sum(.emoji_token_estimate))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   emoji bytes codepoints est_tokens
#>   <int> <int>      <int>      <int>
#> 1  1454  6551       1706       3300

emoji_sanitize() then applies one named policy to the column. The capability is not new – most of it exists across emoji_to_text() and the extraction verbs – but the named argument shows up in a script diff and in a methods section, which is the point:

demo_llm <- data.frame(text = "ship it \U0001f680 today")
for (p in c("keep", "strip", "name", "shortcode", "placeholder")) {
  cat(format(p, width = 12), emoji_sanitize(demo_llm, text, policy = p)$text,
      "\n")
}
#> keep         ship it 🚀 today 
#> strip        ship it today 
#> name         ship it rocket today 
#> shortcode    ship it :rocket: today 
#> placeholder  ship it [emoji] today

Those five policies are not interchangeable: they lose different amounts of information, and only one of them can be undone after the model call. vignette("reversible-preprocessing", package = "tidyEmoji") works through that round trip on the cases that break a hand-rolled substitution, and shows how to keep the emoji signal as feature columns while the text you send holds no emoji at all.

Auditing the emoji a model writes

The same verbs work on emoji a model produces. A transcript of model output is a text column, so “how much emoji does this assistant use, where, and of what kind?” needs nothing new: emoji_ratio() finds the replies that are nothing but emoji, emoji_position() whether the emoji close a reply, emoji_type() the faces against the objects, and emoji_trend() over a model-version column whether an update changed the register. Work on around a million chatbot conversations treats exactly this, the emoji in the model’s turns, as part of how the model positions itself towards the user.

replies <- data.frame(
  model = c("v1", "v1", "v2", "v2"),
  reply = c("Sure, here is the summary.",
            "Done \U0001F44D",
            "Great question! \U0001F60A Here you go \U0001F680",
            "\U0001F389\U0001F389")
)
replies %>%
  emoji_ratio(reply) %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(replies = n(), with_emoji = sum(.emoji_n > 0),
            emoji_only = sum(.emoji_only, na.rm = TRUE),
            emoji = sum(.emoji_n), codepoints = sum(.emoji_codepoints))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   model replies with_emoji emoji_only emoji codepoints
#>   <chr>   <int>      <int>      <int> <int>      <int>
#> 1 v1          2          1          0     1          1
#> 2 v2          2          2          1     4          4

Recording provenance

“Emoji” is not a fixed object. Which glyphs exist, what they are called and which lexicon scored them all depend on versions, and a result is not reproducible without them. emoji_provenance() puts the lot in one row you can paste into a methods section:

emoji_provenance() %>% glimpse()
#> Rows: 1
#> Columns: 8
#> $ tidyEmoji          <chr> "0.7.0"
#> $ emoji_pkg          <chr> "16.0.0"
#> $ unicode_emoji      <chr> "18.0"
#> $ unicode_emoji_date <date> 2026-04-30
#> $ n_emoji            <int> 5244
#> $ sentiment_lexicon  <chr> "novak2015 (969 emoji)"
#> $ emotion_lexicon    <chr> "emotag1200 (150 emoji)"
#> $ R                  <chr> "4.6.2"

Bundled datasets

tidyEmoji ships six datasets, each documented with its own help page:

  • oasst_messages and oasst_reactions: the example corpus used throughout this vignette, 1,485 messages from OpenAssistant Conversations with their dates, roles and languages, and the reaction tallies on them (see ?oasst_messages).
  • emoji_sentiment_lexicon: emoji sentiment scores from the Emoji Sentiment Ranking (see ?emoji_sentiment_lexicon).
  • emoji_emotion_lexicon: emoji emotion scores from EmoTag1200 (see ?emoji_emotion_lexicon).
  • emoji_unicode_crosswalk: one row per (name, glyph) pair, mapping names / shortcodes to glyphs and categories. The mapping is many-to-many both ways, so join on key rather than emoji_name unless you want the duplicates (see ?emoji_unicode_crosswalk).
  • category_unicode_crosswalk: one row per Unicode category, listing its emoji.

The emoji catalogue itself is internal and is surfaced by emoji_properties(). It and the two crosswalks are rebuilt from Unicode’s emoji-test.txt (with the shortcodes taken from the emoji package), and the two lexicons from their published sources, by the scripts in the data-raw/ directory of the package’s source repository, as is the example corpus from OASST2. That directory is not part of the installed package.

Hanson L, Lahrim E, Tong X (2026). EmojiSentR: An R Package for Integrated Text and Emoji Sentiment Analysis. Journal of Behavioral Data Science 6(1). https://doi.org/10.35566/jbds/tonghl.

Miller H, Thebault-Spieker J, Chang S, Johnson I, Terveen L, Hecht B (2016). “Blissfully Happy” or “Ready to Fight”: Varying Interpretations of Emoji. ICWSM 2016. The source of the disagreement result behind emoji_ambiguity(), and of the polarisation measure.
